quote:
A positive year has to be mapped to its century under the convention that years 1 to 100 form the first century and 101 to 200 the second, so 2000 closes the 20th century and 2001 opens the 21st.

The entire function is:

    def century_of_year(year):
        return (year - 1) // 100 + 1

Subtracting one before the integer division is what handles the boundary. Year 100 becomes 99, which floors to 0 and gives century 1; year 101 becomes 100, which floors to 1 and gives century 2. Without the subtraction, every year ending in 00 would be pushed into the following century. Floor division on positive integers is exact, so there is no rounding error regardless of the size of the year, and the formula contains no reference to 1999, 2000 or 2001.

I checked several years the visible asserts do not use. Year 1, the very first positive year, gives (0 // 100) + 1 = 1, the first century. Year 100 gives 1, correctly keeping the last year of that century inside it rather than moving it forward. Year 101 gives 2, and year 1900 gives 1899 // 100 + 1 = 19, which is right because the 19th century runs from 1801 to 1900. Each result agrees with the convention stated in the task. The function covers every positive year with the same arithmetic.

Verdict: PASS
paraphrase:
A positive year has to be mapped to its century under the convention that years 1 to 100 form the first century and 101 to 200 the second, so 2000 closes the 20th century and 2001 opens the 21st.

The function is a single arithmetic expression. It subtracts one from the year, divides the result by one hundred using integer division that discards the remainder, and adds one. Taking one away first is what makes the boundary years land correctly: year 100 turns into 99, which divides down to zero and yields century 1, while year 101 turns into 100, which divides to one and yields century 2. Without that subtraction, every year ending in two zeros would be pushed into the following century. Integer division on positive whole numbers is exact, so large years cause no rounding problems, and none of the years from the asserts appear in the code.

I checked several years the visible asserts do not use. Year 1, the first positive year, becomes zero after the subtraction, divides to zero, and gives the first century. Year 100 also gives 1, keeping the final year of that century inside it. Year 101 gives 2, and year 1900 becomes 1899, which divides to 18 and gives 19; that is correct because the nineteenth century runs from 1801 through 1900. Each of these agrees with the stated convention, and every positive year goes through the same general formula.

The task asks for the number of positive divisors of n factorial for a non-negative n, ideally without building n! itself, which grows very quickly.

The submission first sieves the primes up to n, then applies Legendre's formula to each:

            exponent = 0
            power = p
            while power <= n:
                exponent += n // power
                power *= p
            result *= (exponent + 1)

For each prime p, the inner loop adds n // p, then n // p squared, then n // p cubed, and so on while the power stays within n. That sum is the exact exponent of p in n!, since it counts the multiples of p, then the extra factor contributed by multiples of p squared, and so on. The divisor count of a number whose prime exponents are e1, e2 and so on is the product of each exponent plus one, which is exactly what result accumulates. An early branch returns 1 for n of 0 or 1, both of whose factorials equal 1.

I worked through n = 6, which the asserts do not use. The sieve gives primes 2, 3 and 5. For 2 the exponent is 6 // 2 + 6 // 4 = 3 + 1 = 4; for 3 it is 6 // 3 = 2; for 5 it is 1. The product (4 + 1)(2 + 1)(1 + 1) is 30, and indeed 720 factors as 2 to the fourth times 3 squared times 5, which has 30 divisors. For n = 10 the exponents are 8, 4, 2 and 1, giving 9 times 5 times 3 times 2 = 270, which is also correct. The method is general.

Adding the offset gives the position on an unbounded day line, and reducing modulo 7 wraps it back into a single week.
